items.title: A mole of marshmallows would cover the USA 600 miles deep
items.claim: 6.022 times 10 to the 23 is just a number until you try to picture it. Avogadro's number of marshmallows would bury the entire surface of the United States to a depth of 600 miles.
items.prompt: Roughly how many moles of water molecules are in a single drop (about 0.05 mL)?

options.text: About 0.003 moles, which is roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules
Around 6 times 10 to the 23 — one drop is one mole
About 0.05 moles, the same as the volume in millilitres

items.reveal_title: Even a microscopic drop contains stupefying numbers of molecules
items.reveal:
0.05 mL of water has a mass of 0.05 g. Water is 18 g per mole, so 0.05 / 18 equals about 0.0028 mol. Multiply by Avogadro's number and you get roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules.

If you counted those molecules at one per second, it would take about 50 trillion years — over 3000 times the age of the universe. Chemistry is the study of mind-bending counts of incredibly tiny things.
items.why: The mole is treated as a unit conversion when it should be treated as a stark statement about scale.

items.title: An atom is about 99.9999999999999 percent empty space
items.claim: If a hydrogen atom were scaled up so the nucleus was the size of a marble (1 cm), the electron would orbit roughly 1 kilometre away. Almost everything 'solid' around you is overwhelmingly empty.
items.prompt: If atoms are mostly empty, why does a wall feel solid?

options.text: Walls have very few atoms in them
Solidity comes from electromagnetic repulsion between electron clouds and from Pauli exclusion preventing electron states from overlapping — not from particles physically touching
Atoms swell up to fill space when forces are applied
The 'empty space' is filled with a dense medium

items.reveal:
A hydrogen atom is about 10 to the minus 10 m across. Its nucleus is about 10 to the minus 15 m. The ratio is 100,000 — so atoms are about 10 to the 15 times more volume than nuclei.

When you touch a table, no atoms touch. Electromagnetic forces between the electron clouds of your fingertip and the wood push back. The Pauli exclusion principle prevents the electrons from sharing identical quantum states, contributing the actual 'incompressibility' of matter.

Rutherford's 1909 gold foil experiment showed this directly — most alphas passed through gold foil unscathed because gold atoms are mostly empty.
items.why: Students treat atoms as small spheres of stuff. They are tiny dense nuclei surrounded by enormous shells of probability.

items.title: Lithium reacts less vigorously than sodium even though it is above it
items.claim: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs all react more violently with water in turn. Yet lithium has the highest ionisation energy AND the most negative standard electrode potential (-3.04 V — even more negative than caesium's -3.03 V).

options.text: Lithium is mislabelled — it should be in Group 2
Reactivity with water is rate-controlled by surface kinetics: lithium has a high melting point and forms a thick LiOH crust, so it reacts slowly even though it is highly thermodynamically active
Lithium doesn't really react with water at all
The standard electrode potential table is wrong

items.reveal:
Standard electrode potential measures the thermodynamic tendency to release electrons in aqueous solution. Lithium's small ion has very high hydration enthalpy (-519 kJ/mol vs caesium's -264), which more than compensates its higher ionisation energy.

But observed reactivity also depends on how fast the metal can deliver electrons. Lithium has a higher melting point (181°C) than sodium (98°C), so it does not melt in the heat of its own reaction with water. The LiOH product is less soluble than NaOH and forms an adherent coating. So lithium fizzes calmly; sodium spits and ignites.

Down the group, melting points drop, hydroxides become more soluble, and surface kinetics dominate.
items.why: Reactivity series is often presented as a single ladder. Real reactivity needs both thermodynamic driving force AND a kinetic pathway.
